pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 7–9; why the poles have extreme seasons — Earth's axis is tilted ~23.5°, so as Earth orbits the Sun each pole spends half the year tilted TOWARD the Sun (continuous daylight, warmer summer) and half tilted AWAY (continuous darkness, bitter winter); this tilt also drives sea ice expanding in winter and retreating in summer and triggers animal migration and breeding.
• Standards—UK: DfE KS2 Y5 'Earth and space' (Earth's rotation to explain day/night; movement relative to the Sun) extended to axial tilt and seasons.
• Standards—US: NGSS 5-ESS1-2 (patterns of daylight from Earth's motion); MS-ESS1-1 (Earth-Sun model for seasons) foreshadowed.
• Operational details: the key move is that seasons come from the TILT, not from Earth being nearer/further from the Sun. Model Earth orbiting with its axis pointing a FIXED direction, so at one point in the orbit the North Pole leans sunward (Arctic summer, midnight sun) and six months later leans away (Arctic polar night). Tie it to consequences: sea ice grows/shrinks with the seasons and animals migrate and breed on that cycle. This is the 'why' behind the 5–7 midnight-sun/polar-night phenomenon.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (7) say Earth is tilted and that's why we have seasons; Tier B (8) explain that a pole tilted toward the Sun has summer/long days and tilted away has winter/long nights; Tier C (9) explain that the tilt (not distance to the Sun) drives the extreme polar seasons and the yearly sea-ice and animal cycles.
bestPractices: Model the axis pointing a FIXED direction all the way round the orbit, so the same tilt produces opposite seasons on opposite sides of the Sun
Confront the distance misconception directly — Earth is actually slightly closer to the Sun in northern winter; it's the TILT that matters
Use a torch-and-tilted-globe demo so children see the toward-Sun pole bathed in light for a full turn (midnight sun)
Link cause to consequences pupils can picture: sea ice expanding/retreating, animals migrating and breeding on the seasonal cycle
Connect back to the 5–7 midnight-sun/polar-night phenomenon as the effect this tilt explains
keyRepresentations: Orbit diagram: Earth at four positions, axis fixed, showing which pole leans sunward
Tilted-globe-and-torch demo with the sunlit pole staying lit through a full spin
Toward-Sun / away-from-Sun pole close-ups labelled summer/midnight-sun and winter/polar-night
Seasonal sea-ice extent animation paired with a migration/breeding calendar
commonMisconceptions: Seasons happen because Earth moves closer to and further from the Sun — it's the axial TILT, not distance
The whole Earth is hot in summer and cold in winter at once — opposite hemispheres have opposite seasons
The axis tips back and forth toward the Sun — it points a fixed direction; Earth's position in orbit changes which pole leans sunward
The Sun goes out in polar winter — that pole is tilted away, so the Sun stays below the horizon
Seasons and sea-ice/animal cycles are unrelated — the same tilt drives the extreme seasons AND the yearly ice and migration cycles

learn.summary: For ages 7–9, explain why the poles have extreme seasons: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5° and points in a FIXED direction as Earth orbits the Sun, so each pole spends half the year leaning toward the Sun (continuous daylight, comparatively warmer summer) and half leaning away (continuous darkness, bitter winter). The seasons come from the tilt, not from Earth's changing distance to the Sun. The same tilt drives sea ice expanding in winter and retreating in summer, and animal cycles of migration and breeding. The preferred build is a 2D orbit a child can drag to see which pole is lit, with linked day/night and sea-ice responses; a 3D fly-around orbit, a tap-to-reveal static diagram, a torch-and-globe demonstration, and targeted multiple-choice checks are offered as alternatives with different purposes, none claimed to be superior.

activities.title: Drag Earth around the Sun with a fixed tilt
feedback: If a learner thinks closer-to-Sun means summer, point to the distance toggle and to a real fact: Earth is actually slightly closer to the Sun in January, during northern winter. The small change in distance does not cause the seasons — the tilt does.
If a learner thinks the axis tips back and forth, replay the loop and highlight that the axis arrow stayed pointing the same way; only Earth's position in the orbit changed which pole leans sunward.
When a pole leans toward the Sun, confirm: long daylight and warmer summer, and the sea-ice gauge shrinks; when it leans away, long darkness and winter, and the sea-ice gauge grows.
If a learner says the Sun goes out in polar winter, clarify the Sun is still shining — that pole is tilted away so the Sun stays below the horizon.
activities.rationale: The target is a spatial cause-and-effect mechanism, so letting the child operate the orbit and see the lit pole, day-clock and sea-ice gauge respond makes the tilt-not-distance causal link concrete, and the distance toggle challenges the distance misconception directly. The linked day-clock and sea-ice gauge are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism visible, not required components.
sourceClaims: Earth's ~23.5° axial tilt, with the axis fixed in direction through the orbit, causes seasons and the polar cycles of continuous summer daylight and winter darkness — not variation in Earth-Sun distance
learnerActions: Grab Earth and drag it all the way around a glowing Sun, noticing that the axis stays locked pointing the same direction for the whole loop.
Watch a spotlight show which pole is bathed in sunlight as Earth moves.

Drag Earth to the position where the North Pole leans into the light and observe a day-clock spinning a full 24 hours with the Sun never setting (Arctic summer, midnight sun) while a sea-ice gauge shrinks.
Drag Earth to the opposite side where the North Pole leans away and observe the Sun never rising, the polar-night scene darkening, and the sea-ice gauge growing.
State in your own words which pole has summer at each position and why.

Use a 'blame the distance?' toggle that briefly moves Earth slightly nearer and further and notice that, in this simplified model, the seasons do not change. In real life, the small change in distance has only a minor effect and is not what causes the seasons.
activities.intendedInsight: The SAME fixed tilt produces summer on one side of the orbit and winter on the other; it is the tilt (combined with orbital position), not distance to the Sun, that makes a pole swing between endless day and endless night.

activities.title: Fly around the orbit in 3D to find the sunward-leaning pole
feedback: If the learner loses track of the tilt direction while rotating the view, pause and trace the axis arrow — it points the same way regardless of your viewpoint.
Confirm that the pole tilted toward the Sun has summer and endless daylight, and the pole tilted away has winter and endless night.
activities.rationale: A 3D fly-around may build spatial intuition by showing the tilt from angles a flat diagram cannot, and is offered as a richer alternative; a well-built 2D orbit conveys the same causal story at lower cost, so 3D is a valuable option rather than a requirement. Comparative efficacy between these formats is not established by the sources.
learnerActions: Move your viewpoint around a 3D Earth-Sun orbit to look at the tilted axis from different angles.

At each of four orbital positions, identify which pole is leaning toward the Sun and which is leaning away. Notice that at the two in-between (equinox) positions, neither pole leans toward the Sun, and both poles get some day and some night.
At the two positions where one pole leans fully toward the Sun, describe how the lit pole experiences continuous daylight and the dark pole continuous night.
activities.intendedInsight: Earth-Sun geometry is genuinely three-dimensional; viewing the tilt from different angles can build spatial intuition for why one pole is bathed in light while the other is in darkness.

activities.title: Four-position orbit diagram with tap-to-reveal labels
feedback: If a learner expects both poles to be warm at once, point out that at the summer and winter positions one pole leans toward the Sun while the other leans away, so opposite hemispheres have opposite seasons. At the two in-between positions, neither pole leans toward the Sun.
Reinforce that the axis arrow points the same direction in all four positions; it is Earth's place in the orbit that changes.
activities.rationale: A labelled static diagram makes the four key orbital positions visible and is useful for consolidation or low-tech settings; because it does not animate the continuous link between orbital position, tilt and sunlight, pair it with hands-on or interactive modelling where possible.
learnerActions: Look at an orbit diagram showing Earth at four positions with its axis drawn in a fixed direction.
Tap each position to reveal whether the North Pole leans toward the Sun, away from it, or neither (sideways to the Sun, at the spring and autumn positions), and the season it causes.
Match each position to 'summer/midnight-sun', 'winter/polar-night' or 'spring/autumn (in-between, with sunrise and sunset)' for the North Pole.
activities.intendedInsight: At different points in the same orbit, the fixed tilt leaves one pole leaning sunward (summer) and later leaning away (winter).

activities.title: Torch-and-tilted-globe demonstration
feedback: If a learner tips the globe to point at the torch each time, stop and reset: the axis must keep pointing the same direction; only your position around the torch changes.
Confirm that the pole in continuous light is having summer and the pole in continuous shadow is having winter.
activities.rationale: A physical torch-and-globe demonstration lets children see the toward-light pole bathed in light for a full turn, which may make the midnight-sun effect tangible. The globe and torch are approximations of the real Earth and Sun and should be kept distinct from the bodies they represent.
learnerActions: Tilt a globe so its axis points a fixed direction, then carry it around a torch standing in for the Sun, keeping the tilt pointing the same way the whole time.
Spin the globe at the position where one pole leans toward the torch and watch that pole stay in the light through a full spin (midnight sun).
Carry the globe to the opposite side and spin it again to see that pole stay in shadow (polar night).
Describe what season each pole is having at each position.
activities.intendedInsight: A pole tilted toward the light source stays lit even as Earth spins, giving continuous daylight; a pole tilted away stays dark, giving continuous night.

activities.title: Check understanding: tilt vs distance and which pole has summer
feedback: If a learner picks 'closer in summer', counter with simultaneity: when the north has summer the south has winter though both are at similar distance from the Sun — so it must be the tilt.
If a learner says the Sun is just brighter/hotter in summer, note the Sun's output is steady; what changes is how directly and how long its light reaches a place, because of the tilt.
Credit answers that link the tilt to sea ice growing in winter and shrinking in summer, or to animals migrating and breeding on the seasonal cycle.
activities.rationale: Short recognition checks can confirm the model has taken hold and surface the distance misconception, but recognition alone does not elicit independent construction of the explanation, so use them after the operable activities rather than to teach.
learnerActions: Answer which-pole-has-summer questions for given orbital positions.
Decide whether tilt or distance explains the seasons, using the fact that opposite hemispheres have opposite seasons at the same time.
Explain how the same tilt links to sea ice spreading in winter and shrinking in summer, and to animal migration or breeding on the yearly cycle.
activities.intendedInsight: A learner who understands credits the axial tilt (not distance) and can connect the seasonal cycle to at least one consequence such as sea-ice change or animal behaviour.

constraints: Model the axis pointing a FIXED direction all the way round the orbit; do not let the axis tip toward and away from the Sun, which seeds the 'wobbling axis' misconception.
Confront the distance misconception directly: Earth is actually slightly closer to the Sun during northern winter, so it is the tilt, not distance, that matters.

Tie cause to consequences children can picture: sea ice expanding/retreating and animals migrating and breeding on the seasonal cycle (meets the requirement to connect to at least one animal behaviour).
Connect back to the midnight-sun / polar-night phenomenon as the effect this tilt explains.

Recognition-only multiple-choice checks do not elicit independent construction of the explanation; use them to confirm, not to build, understanding — they are not claimed to be superior to the other formats.
A static diagram does not animate the continuous link between orbital position, tilt and sunlight; treat it as a consolidation scaffold and pair with hands-on or interactive modelling.
Globes, torches and screen orbits are approximations of the real Earth and Sun; keep the represented bodies distinct from the models.
Make clear the Sun does not go out in polar winter — the pole is tilted away so the Sun stays below the horizon.

The distance toggle's 'nothing changes' result is an age-appropriate idealisation; Earth's distance to the Sun does vary slightly through the year, but that small effect is dominated by and distinct from the tilt.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The three listed sources are marked verified:false in the row; curriculum and NASA/Royal Museums Greenwich references support the tilt-causes-seasons principle but do not establish comparative efficacy or necessity of any particular medium.

sourceClaims were kept only on the 2D drag activity, because that activity directly demonstrates and tests the sourced tilt-not-distance principle via the distance toggle; they were set to [] on the 3D, static-diagram, torch-globe and check activities, whose rationales concern medium choice, viewpoint, tangibility or check timing, which no source claim supports.
Legacy fit rationales asserting a static image 'can't animate' the dynamic link and that open dialogue is 'poorly served' were reframed as scoped observable limits, not universal pedagogical laws.

The row's distance point is physically sound for a 7–9 audience: both hemispheres are at similar Sun distance at a given time and Earth is actually slightly nearer the Sun in northern winter; this was retained as the key counter to the distance misconception.

probeDeeper: When it's summer at the North Pole, what season is it at the South Pole — and are they different distances from the Sun right then?
If distance caused seasons, both poles would be warm at the same time. Are they? What does that tell you?
Which way is a pole tilted during its months of endless daylight — toward or away from the Sun?
How does the same tilt explain sea ice spreading in winter and shrinking in summer?
assess.correctAnswer: No — seasons are NOT caused by the Earth getting closer to or farther from the Sun. They are caused by the TILT of the Earth's axis (about 23.5°). As the Earth orbits the Sun, each pole spends half the year tilted TOWARD the Sun — giving continuous daylight and the warmer polar summer — and half tilted AWAY — giving continuous darkness and bitter winter. (In fact both hemispheres are at similar distances from the Sun at the same time, and it's the tilt, not distance, that gives one summer while the other has winter.) The same tilt drives sea ice growing in winter and shrinking in summer, and animal behaviours like migration and breeding.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Seasons are caused by Earth's distance from the Sun (closer=summer)' — the classic distance misconception.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Counter with simultaneity: when the north has summer the south has winter, though both are the same distance from the Sun. It must be the TILT, not distance.
errorPatterns.distractor: In summer the Earth is much closer to the Sun, and in winter it's much farther away.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Explains summer/winter by the Earth moving nearer/farther from the Sun.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The Earth's tilt changes back and forth through the year' — thinks the axis wobbles rather than pointing steadily.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model it: the axis stays pointed the same direction all year; it's the POSITION in orbit that puts a given pole toward or away from the Sun.
errorPatterns.distractor: The Earth tips toward the Sun in summer and tips away in winter.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the Earth tilts toward the Sun then tilts the other way; doesn't grasp a fixed axis pointing the same way while orbiting.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The Sun is just brighter/hotter in summer' — attributes seasons to the Sun changing, not Earth's geometry.
errorPatterns.nextMove: The Sun's output is steady; what changes is how directly and for how long its light reaches a given place, due to the tilt.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the Sun gives out more heat in summer.

responseLevels.gap: Attributes seasons to the Earth's distance from the Sun, or to the Sun changing.
responseLevels.full: Explains seasons by the fixed ~23.5° axial tilt — a pole tilted toward the Sun gets continuous daylight/summer, tilted away gets continuous dark/winter — rejects the distance idea using opposite-hemisphere seasons, and links the tilt to the sea-ice cycle.
responseLevels.partial: Mentions the tilt but can't explain how toward/away in orbit gives months of light or dark, or still lets distance creep in.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: The poles have extreme seasons — a summer of endless daylight, a winter of endless dark. A student says 'that's because in summer the Earth is much CLOSER to the Sun, and in winter it's much farther away.' Is it distance from the Sun that causes the seasons? If not, what does — and why does that give a pole months of daylight then months of dark?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: This targets the classic, robust 'distance causes seasons' misconception. A student holding it credits closeness/farness; a student with the concept credits the axial tilt and can explain toward/away producing months of light or dark. The counter (both hemispheres at similar distance, yet opposite seasons) is decisive.

sources.claim: KS2 Y5 pupils use the idea of Earth's rotation and movement relative to the Sun to explain day/night and related phenomena
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum, Science Y5 'Earth and space'

sources.claim: Students represent Earth's motion to explain patterns of daylight and, later, seasons via axial tilt

Earth's ~23.5° axial tilt, with the axis fixed in direction through the orbit, causes seasons and the polar cycles of continuous summer daylight and winter darkness — not variation in Earth-Sun distance
